CODING CHALLENGES
Although this book has been very helpful
in guiding readers and students to learn
several aspects of Unity over the years,
many of my students have had difficulty
transitioning from the tutorials in the
book to creating their own games from
scratch.
This chapter introduces you to the
Coding Challenges that I have developed
over the past few years to help with that
transition, and I will continue adding
more challenges every year.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

What Is a Coding Challenge?
Previous editions of this book presented you with the series of tutorials in Part III and
then wished you luck as you set off to create your own games. Over the years since pub-
lishing the first edition of this book, I found that to be a daunting task for both readers
and students. The blank white page (or empty Unity project) can be very intimidating.
Happily, based on a recommendation by my longtime teaching assistant Ellie Locatis,
we started developing Coding Challenges that I have used for students in my class over
the past few years. I have found these to be an excellent transitional tool between the
tutorials in the book and you creating your own games.
At the midpoint of every semester that I teach my Introduction to Game and Interac-
tive Media Development class, I find that even very good students often feel like they
may understand the code that they've written from the book, but they don't think they
know how to create code themselves. Since we've started using them, these Coding
Challenges have become the point where students can start feeling confident in their
own programming abilities. The more of these challenges you tackle and complete, the
more you will see that you do understand how to translate your games from concepts to
code, and the more you will be prepared to develop your own games.
Figure 37.1 The Updraft game after you complete it, showing mountains, clouds, an updraft, and the
boost gauge
To create each of these challenges, I first built a simple game in Unity. After completing
the game—including tuning all the variables in the Inspector—I went back and replaced
the content of every method with code comments describing each step taken in that

Getting Started on a Coding Challenge
Go to this book's website at http://book.prototools.net and look under Coding
Challenges. There you will find an ever-growing library of challenges for you to tackle.
The Updraft challenge that I feature in this chapter is the first that I developed to this
level of detail, but I will continue adding more challenges every year.
Figure 37.2 The Updraft project after the Starter Kit has been imported
On the book website, you will find the following for each challenge:
■ A Starter Kit UnityPackage: Figure 37.2 shows the Updraft project immediately
after you import the Updraft Starter Kit. All Starter Kits contain:
■ All the art assets needed for the challenge
■ A ReadMe file that will automatically open in the Inspector (shown on the right
side of Figure 37.2) that includes the parameters of the challenge, a link to a
playable version of the game, and a brief description of gameplay

■ A pre-configured Scene with all the proper settings in the Inspector and all the
GameObjects set up correctly
■ Several carefully commented scripts with methods that you will need to write
yourself
■ A license that clarifies your use of the Starter Kit and its assets, including what
you may and may not do with them
■ A playable version of the game (usually as a WebGL): Though the Starter
Kit ReadMe briefly describes the gameplay, you'll get a much better idea of how the
game works from playing the WebGL for some time.
■ An indication of the Unity Project Template you should use: This will usually
be 3D Core, but I make it clear if that isn't the case.
■ Several C# scripts: The C# scripts in each Coding Challenge include copious com-
ments and notes describing what the code needs to do in each script. You will not
need to add any public fields to any script, because all of these have been provided
for you and had their values set in the Unity Inspector.
Your job in each challenge is to fill in the blanks in the scripts with working code.

As you're working on these, remember that it's not important how pretty your code is
or if it looks exactly like mine—there are myriad ways that you could have written differ-
ent code and still achieved the same behavior—it is important that the game works the
same way as the playable version on the book's website.
How to Approach Each Challenge
It usually helps to tackle each challenge in the same way:
1. Read the description of the game on the http://book.prototools.net website.
2. Spend some time with the playable WebGL version of the game. Get a feel for how
the game works and start thinking now about changes that you might want to make
to the game once you've got it working.

3. Follow the Standard Project Setup Procedure in Appendix A to get a new, empty
project based on the correct template (usually 3D Core). (Now is also the time to
make your initial commit to version control, if you're using it.)
4. Download the Starter Kit and import it into your new Unity project.
5. Familiarize yourself with all the assets imported by the Starter Kit and the scripts that
you'll need to implement. Take the time now to understand what each of the scripts
does in the game.
6. Start small. Although it's tempting in the Updraft project to jump right in and start
programming the PlaneControls.cs script, that's also the most complex script in the
game. Pick one of the smaller scripts and get it working first.
One caveat is that you might need one script so you can test another: In the
8pdraft class, Reposition() is called on any Updraft GameObject whenever the
plane exits it; so without the PlaneControls.cs script, you can't fly through an updraft
to test it. On the other hand, there is often a way to test even without the other
script. For example, if you implement the 8pdraft class as shown in Code Listing
37.2, press Play in Unity, and then use Unity's move tool to move the plane through
the Updraft, the 8pdraft script will receive an 2nTriggerE[it() call, allowing you
to test the script.
7. Work progressively. Don't try to implement an entire script at once; just get a
little bit working and then try testing. Continuing the example of the 8pdraft class,

8. Frequently test and push to version control, if you're using it. You don't want to
lose any work, and version control can ensure that you have a history of backups.
9. After you've completed the challenge, take a snapshot of the completed
project. For my students, this means making a WebGL build and pushing a commit
to version control. It's always good to have a completed challenge archived before
moving on to…
10. Make it your own. Now that you've completed the challenge, think back to when
you played it (step 2) and come up with changes and improvements that you would
like to make. This step is one of the most critical for increasing your confidence in
your coding and design abilities.
11. And, of course, have fun! You're learning to make games, and I sincerely hope that
you're having a great time doing it.

BEYOND THIS BOOK
You've read about game design, finished all
the tutorials, and completed some Coding
Challenges. So, what's next?
Now is the time to start developing your own
game projects! In this brief chapter, I give you
some tips on doing so.

Continue to Learn Unity Development
After my introductory game development class—for which I use this book—I teach an
Advanced Game Development class that is focused around one specific goal: teaching
the students how to learn independently. I've taught several different iterations of
advanced game programming classes, and this is—by far—the most successful. The great
news is that you can do the core exercise of the class on your own and learn almost as
much from it.
Here are the steps to a standard project assignment in my advanced game program-
ming class:
1. Choose a topic that you want to learn about. Some of the most popular ones in my
class have been:
■ Visual Scripting in Unity: Using Shader Graph, VFX Graph, or Bolt
■ Procedural Content Generation: Using layers of various noise functions to
generate images, terrain, dungeons, caves, or even music
■ Game AI (Artificial Intelligence): I highly recommend any of the excellent
articles at http://www.gameaipro.com/
■ Animation in Unity: https://docs.unity3d.com/2020.3/Documentation/
Manual/AnimationSection.html

similar to Cascading Style Sheets in web design, https://docs.unity3d.com/
2020.3/Documentation/Manual/UIElements.html
■ Unity's Data-Oriented Tech Stack (DOTS): https://unity.com/dots (and see

2. Find a good online tutorial to start from. There are many excellent video tutorials
available from Unity's Learn website (https://unity.com/learn) or YouTube (https://
youtube.com).
3. Finish the tutorial and reflect on what you learned from it (this is the point at which
we do "research phase" presentations in my class).
4. Decide on something specific you want to do that builds on top of what you learned
in the tutorial.
5. Make it so. Dig into the project you made for the tutorial and transform it into what
you want. This is a great time to look into other tutorials and see if you can merge
knowledge from them into your project. This is what we call the "creative phase" in
my class, and it's about two-thirds of the total time spent on each project.

This approach has worked consistently to grow my students' skills and their ability to
rapidly acquire new skills. I'm certain it will work for you as well.
Build a Classic Game
I often suggest this to my students. When you're developing an entirely new game, you
are required to both code a game and design it at the same time. Each of these tasks is
difficult enough on its own, so I recommend that your first project after this book be to
re-create a classic game. We usually pick games from the Nintendo Entertainment Sys-
tem era because they have clear mechanics that you can see and understand as you play
them. Some games that tend to be particularly good are Metroid, Mega Man 2,
The Legend of Zelda II (you already made something similar to the first Zelda game in
the Dungeon Delver project), Castlevania, Contra, Punch-Out!!, Ninja Gaiden, Double
Dragon, and Duck Tales.
1
If you're unsure about building one of these from scratch, first
try implementing some of the gadgets or enemies from the first Legend of Zelda game in
your Dungeon Delver project from Part III.
Start a Small Game Project or
Prototype
Go back and check out my advice at the end of Chapter 15, "The Digital Game Industry."
There I list six critical elements you need to have to start working on a game:
1. The Right Idea
2. The Right Scope
3. The Right Team
4. The Right Schedule
5. The Right Ways to Communicate
6. The Will to Finish
I stand by all of these, even if you're just going to be working by yourself. Give your-
self manageable, progressive goals. Don't expect immediate progress, and don't beat
yourself up if you have to go back and redo something— everyone refactors code, and
doing so always improves the code and its readability. The important things are to get
something working and to get feedback from other people playing it.
1. For your first project, I recommend avoiding the following because they are all more challeng-

Make Games for Lifelong Enrichment
In 2015, my friend Chris DeLeon started an online game development training com-
munity that is now called HomeTeam GameDev (http://HomeTeamGameDev.com). His
concept was to create a space where members approached game development in much
the same way that members of a martial arts studio would treat their martial art. They
focus on:
■ Personal improvement regardless of whether it leads to a career
■ Collaboration, with everyone pushing each other to get better
■ Consistent commitment to the project and the other members
■ Education and improvement over product (while still releasing more than 130 games
in just six years)
■ Sustainable practices that avoid burnout
Many readers of this book want game development to be their career, but that's not the
only option. You can also make games in a consistent, sustainable way just because it's
challenging and enjoyable.
Consider Going to School for GameDev
On the other hand, if you know that you want game development to be your career,
and you want to find a way into a studio, one of the best things you can do is to attend a
highly ranked university game development program. This is true at either the under-
graduate or graduate level. Not only can you find excellent people to work with, you
can also make connections that can help you get your foot in the door for interviews at
various game companies.
In 2005, I had been working for several years as a programmer (mostly of Macromedia
Director and Flash) in Austin, Texas. I had developed a pretty good local reputation as a
programmer and had started teaching game development classes at local universities,
but I was interested in a few things that I couldn't easily do in Austin:
■ Transitioning my role from programming to game design
■ Finding a way into game companies outside of Austin
■ Eventually teaching game development full time
I looked at a few different graduate programs and chose the Entertainment Technol-
ogy Center (ETC) at Carnegie Mellon, which was recommended by a close friend and
at the time seemed to have the best combination of practicality, cost (in terms of both
money and time commitment), and industry connections. Within one year, I was being

Explore Advanced Game Design
My good friend and mentor Michael Sellers wrote a fantastic book about systems design
titled Advanced Game Design: A Systems Approach.
2
Mike is a longtime industry veteran
who designed the first 3D MMO (Meridian 59) and wrote the AI for Sims 2 that deter-
mined how other sims in the room would react when two sims were arguing, kissing,
etc. He was also lead designer on Ultima Online. Since 2017, Mike has been the Direc-
tor of the Game Design program at Indiana University Bloomington. The methods and
knowledge in his book have been battle tested both in the industry and in the class-
room, and I cannot more highly recommend it.
I also recommend checking out any of the other books that I listed in the Preface. They
are all excellent. I'm specifically mentioning Mike's book now because it is the only one
that was intentionally written as a follow-up to this book.
Finally, Drop Me a Line
If you enjoyed this book—or even if you didn't—I'd like to hear from you. There's a
contact form on the book's website that goes directly to me, or you can email me at jer-
emy@prototools.net. I've put a ridiculous amount of time into this book, and I'm always
happy to hear how it has helped you and/or how I can make it better. Thank you for the
time you spent reading it.
